{{Short description|Moduli space of the Yang–Mills equations}}
In [[gauge theory]], the '''Yang–Mills moduli space''' (short '''YM moduli space''', also '''instanton moduli space''') is the [[moduli space]] of the [[Yang–Mills equations]], hence the space of its solutions up to gauge. It is used in [[Donaldson's theorem]], proven in {{harv|Donaldson|1983}} and improved in {{harv|Donaldson|1987}}, which was listed as a contribution for [[Simon Donaldson]] winning the [[Fields Medal]] in 1986, and to defined the [[Donaldson invariant|Donaldson invariants]] used to study four-dimensional smooth manifolds (short 4-manifolds). A difficulity is, that the Yang–Mills moduli space is usually not [[Compact space|compact]] and has to be [[Compactification (mathematics)|compactified]] around singularities through laborious techniques. An improvement later appeared with the always compact [[Seiberg–Witten moduli space]]. The Yang–Mills moduli space is named after [[Chen-Ning Yang]] and [[Robert Mills (physicist)|Robert Mills]], who introduced the underlying Yang–Mills equations in 1954.

In four dimensions, see also [[four-dimensional Yang–Mills theory]], important subspaces of the Yang-Mills moduli space are the '''self-dual Yang-Mills moduli space''' (short '''SDYM moduli space''', also '''self-dual instanton moduli space''') of solutions of the [[self-dual Yang-Mills equations]] up to gauge and the '''anti self-dual Yang-Mills moduli space''' (short '''ASDYM moduli space''', also '''anti self-dual instanton moduli space''') of solutions of the [[anti self-dual Yang-Mills equations]] up to gauge.

== Definition ==
Let <math>G</math> be a [[Lie group]] with [[Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> and <math>\pi\colon P\twoheadrightarrow X</math> be a [[Principal bundle|principal <math>G</math>-bundle]] over a [[smooth manifold]] <math>X</math>, which automatically makes <math>P</math> a [[smooth manifold]] as well. Let <math>\operatorname{Ad}(P):=P\times_G\mathfrak{g}</math> be the [[adjoint bundle]], then the [[Yang–Mills equations]] as well as the (anti) self-dual Yang–Mills equations are formulated on the configuration space:

: <math>
\mathcal{A}
=\Omega^1(X,\operatorname{Ad}(P))
\cong\Omega_{\operatorname{Ad}}^1(P,\mathfrak{g})
</math>

where the isomorphism requires a choice of local sections <math>s_i\colon U_i\hookrightarrow P</math> for an open cover <math>(U_i)_{i\in I}\subset X</math> (or alternatively a connection since the latter space is an affine vector space, which makes the isomorphism non-canonical) and is then given by:

: <math>
\Omega_{\operatorname{Ad}}^1(P,\mathfrak{g})\xrightarrow\cong\Omega^1(X,\operatorname{Ad}(P)),
A\mapsto(s_i^*A)_{i\in I}.
</math>

Since the configuration space is an infinite-dimensional [[vector space]], it is more difficult to handle. But also due to the group action on the principal bundle, it is plausible to consider a [[group action]] on the configuration space with the following gauge group:

: <math>
\mathcal{G}
:= C^\infty(P,G)^G
\cong C^\infty(X,G)
\cong\operatorname{Aut}(P)
</math>

where the isomorphisms are given using the free and transitive action of <math>G</math> on the fibers of <math>P</math> (with <math>G</math> as a superscript meaning the <math>G</math>-equivariant maps and which are canonical):

: <math>
C^\infty(X,G)\xrightarrow\cong\operatorname{Aut}(P),
f\mapsto(p\mapsto p\cdot f(\pi(p)));
</math>
: <math>
C^\infty(P,G)^G\xrightarrow\cong\operatorname{Aut}(P),
f\mapsto(p\mapsto p\cdot f(p)).
</math>

A principal bundle [[automorphism]] <math>P\rightarrow P</math> induces a vector bundle automorphism <math>\operatorname{Ad}(P)\rightarrow\operatorname{Ad}(P)</math>, causing the gauge group <math>\mathcal{G}</math> to act free on the configuration space <math>\mathcal{A}</math> and resulting in the [[orbit space]]:<ref>Donaldson & Kronheimer 1990, Eq. (4.2.1)</ref><ref name=":5">Naber 11, p. 352</ref>

: <math>
\mathcal{B}
:=\mathcal{A}/\mathcal{G}.
</math>

It can be shown that the Yang–Mills equations are gauge invariant and hence are formulated over just this orbit space. Its solution form the Yang–Mills moduli space:<ref>Uhlenbeck & Freed 1984, p. 10</ref>

: <math>
\mathcal{M}_P
:=\{[A]\in\mathcal{B}|\mathrm{d}_A\star F_A=0\}.
</math>

If <math>X</math> is a [[4-manifold]], then [[four-dimensional Yang–Mills theory]] furthermore allows the definition of the (anti) self-dual Yang–Mills moduli space:<ref>Donaldson & Kronheimer 1990, Chapter 6 on p. 126</ref><ref name=":5" />

: <math>
\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{ASD}
:=\{[A]\in\mathcal{B}|\star F_A=-F_A\};
</math>
: <math>
\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
:=\{[A]\in\mathcal{B}|\star F_A=+F_A\}.
</math>

(While notations like <math>\mathcal{M}_P^-</math> or <math>\mathcal{M}_P^+</math> can also be used, it can be confusing as the (anti) self-dual Yang–Mills equations <math>
\star F_A=\pm F_A
</math> can also be written as <math>
F_A^\mp=0
</math> with the sign in the notation reversed.) There are canonical inclusions <math>\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{ASD},\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}\hookrightarrow\mathcal{M}_P^+</math>. The intersection <math>\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{ASD}\cap\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}</math> includes exactly the [[flat connections]], the [[Critical point (mathematics)|critical points]] of the Chern–Simons action functional, and could therefore be referred to as Chern–Simons moduli space.

== Properties ==

* The anti self-dual Yang–Mills moduli space of a [[principal SU(2)-bundle]] over a Riemannian 4-manifold is orientable.<ref>Donaldson & Kronheimer 1990, Proposition 5.4.1</ref> This more generally holds for principal <math>\operatorname{SU}(n)</math>-bundles.<ref>Donaldson & Kronheimer 1990, 5.4.3</ref>
* The self-dual Yang–Mills moduli space of a principal <math>
\operatorname{SO}(3)
</math>-bundle <math>
P\twoheadrightarrow X
</math> with <math>
p_2(P)[X]\leq 3
</math> over a compact orientable Riemannian 4-manifold <math>
X
</math> is compact.<ref>Uhlenbeck & Freed 1984, Theorem 10.9</ref>
* If <math>X</math> is a [[4-manifold]], then:<ref name=":4">Donaldson 1983, p. 290</ref><ref>Donaldson 1987, Eq. (2.1)</ref><ref>Freed & Uhlenbeck 1991, Equation (2.28)</ref>

:: <math>
\dim\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
=2p_1(\operatorname{Ad}(P))[X]
-\dim G(1-b_1+b_2^-).
</math>
:* In particular for <math>G=\operatorname{SU}(2)</math> the second [[special unitary group]]:<ref name=":0">Freed & Uhlenbeck 1991, Between equations (2.28) and (2.29) on page 42</ref><ref name=":1">Donaldson & Kronheimer 1990, Equation (4.2.21)</ref>
::: <math>
\dim\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
=-8c_2(P)[X]
-3(1-b_1+b_2^-).
</math>
:* In particular for <math>G=\operatorname{SO}(3)</math> the third [[special orthogonal group]]:<ref name=":2">Freed & Uhlenbeck 1991, Equation (2.29) on page 42 & Equation (10.3) on page 155</ref><ref name=":3">Donaldson & Kronheimer 1990, Equation (4.2.22)</ref>
::: <math>
\dim\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
=2p_1(P)[X]
-3(1-b_1+b_2^-).
</math>
It is important to consider the different sign conventions regarding the [[Characteristic class|characteristic classes]] in the first term: ''Instantons and Four-Manifolds'' uses the convention here, while the later ''The Geometry of Four-Manifolds'' uses the reverse convention.

== Application ==

=== Self-dual SU(2) moduli space ===
For the proof of [[Donaldson's theorem]], [[Simon Donaldson]] considered the self-dual Yang–Mills moduli space <math>
\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
</math> of the unique [[principal SU(2)-bundle]] <math>
P\twoheadrightarrow X
</math> with <math>
c_2(P)[X]=-1
</math> over a [[Simply connected space|simply connected]] Riemannian 4-manifold <math>
X
</math> with negative definite intersection form <math>
\omega
</math>. (Over the [[4-sphere]] <math>
S^4
</math>, this would be the quaternionic [[Hopf fibration]] <math>
S^7\twoheadrightarrow S^4
</math>.) After first assuming simple connectedness for <math>
b_1(X)=0
</math> in {{harv|Donaldson|1983}}, he expanded the proof to also work without it in {{harv|Donaldson|1987}}. If the [[intersection form]] <math>
\omega
</math> is definite, then furthermore <math>
b_2^+(X)=0
</math>. According to the above formula,<ref name=":0" /><ref name=":1" /> the self-dual Yang–Mills moduli space <math>
\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
</math> is five-dimensional. Simon Donaldson then gave the following description of its singularities and its boundary, resulting in a [[Cobordism|bordism]] essential for his proof:<ref name=":6">Freed & Uhlenbeck 1984, p. 45-46</ref>
[[File:Donaldson's Theorem cobordism.png|thumb|Visualization<ref name=":6" /><ref>Donaldson & Kronheimer 1990, p. 326</ref> of the Yang–Mills moduli space used in the proof of Donaldson's theorem]]

* If there are <math>
n
</math> pairs <math>
\pm\alpha\in H^2(X,\mathbb{Z})
</math> to the equation <math>
\omega(\alpha,\alpha)=\langle\alpha^2,[X]\rangle=1
</math> with the [[Kronecker pairing]] and [[fundamental class]], then there are <math>
n
</math> singularities <math>
x_1,\ldots,x_n\in\mathcal{M}_P^+
</math>, so that <math>
\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}\setminus\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}
</math> is a [[5-manifold]]. Every such singularity <math>
x_i\in\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
</math> has a neighborhood <math>
U_i\subset\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
</math> diffeomorphic to a [[Cone (topology)|cone]] over the second [[complex projective space]] <math>
\mathbb{C}P^2
</math> (whose tip corresponds to the singularity).
* There exists a neighborhood of the boundary <math>
\partial\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
</math> which is [[Diffeomorphism|diffeomorphic]] to a half-open cylinder over <math>
X
</math>, meaning that <math>
\overline\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
:=\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}\cup X
</math> yields a [[Compactification (mathematics)|compactification]] with <math>
\partial\overline\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
=X
</math>. (A similar approach also works for other negative Chern classes (or positive in the convention of ''The Geometry of Four-Manifolds'').<ref>Donaldson & Kronheimer 1990, Theorem (4.4.3)</ref>) If additionally the cones around the singularities are removed, then <math>
\overline\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}\setminus(U_1\cup\ldots\cup U_n)
</math> describes a [[bordism]] between <math>
X
</math> and <math>
(\mathbb{C}P^2)^{\sqcup n}
</math>. It is important, that all second complex projective spaces have the same orientation, since <math>
\mathbb{C}P^2\sqcup\overline{\mathbb{C}P^2}
</math> is nullbordant (as the boundary the [[5-manifold]] <math>
\mathbb{C}P^2\times[0,1]
</math>) and hence could be canceled out. Since the signature is invariant under bordisms and transfers [[Disjoint union|disjoint unions]] into sums, one has <math>
\sigma(X)
=n\sigma(\mathbb{C}P^2)
=n
</math>.

=== Self-dual SO(3) moduli space ===
[[Ronald Fintushel|Ron Fintushel]] and [[Ronald J. Stern]] considered the self-dual Yang–Mills moduli space <math>
\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
</math> of a principal <math>
\operatorname{SO}(3)
</math>-bundle <math>
P\twoheadrightarrow X
</math> with <math>
p_2(P)[X]=2
</math> over a [[Simply connected space|simply connected]] Riemannian 4-manifold <math>
X
</math> with negative definite intersection form <math>
\omega
</math>. As before, <math>
b_1(X)=0
</math> and <math>
b_1(X)=0
</math>. According to the above formula,<ref name=":2" /><ref name=":3" /> the self-dual Yang–Mills moduli space <math>
\mathcal{M}_P^\mathrm{SD}
</math> is one-dimensional.
